kunyah: Dhat an-Nitaqayn — She of the Two Belts
teaser: She fed the two men in the cave, and took Abu Jahl's blow rather than say where her father had gone.

layers.title: Who She Was
layers.subtitle: A daughter of the house where it all began
layers.content:
Asma bint Abi Bakr as-Siddiq, of Banu Taym ibn Murra — a clan that sat at the edge of Qurayshi power and made its living in cloth and credit rather than in politics.

Her mother was Qutayla bint Abd al-Uzza, whom Abu Bakr had parted from before Islam. That makes Asma the full sister of Abdullah ibn Abi Bakr and the half-sister of Aishah, and it means she was already a young woman while Aishah was still a child.

Ibn Sa'd introduces her and her brother in a single line: Abu Bakr's children were Abdullah, and Asma of the two belts. The title arrives ahead of the story that produced it, as though the compilers assumed every reader already knew.

She married az-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, who owned almost nothing when he married her. Ibn Sa'd's register of az-Zubayr's twenty children names eight of them as hers: Abdullah, Urwa, al-Mundhir, Asim, al-Muhajir, Khadija the elder, Umm al-Hasan and Aishah.

Read Vol. III closely and you notice something beyond the genealogy. She is not only described in it, she speaks in it. Chain after chain runs: Hisham ibn Urwa, from his father, from Asma bint Abi Bakr. Her son Urwa became one of the great scholars of Madinah, and a good deal of what he knew about the first years he had directly from his mother.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley — the entries on Abu Bakr as-Siddiq and az-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam

layers.title: The Conversion
layers.subtitle: There was no night on which she changed her mind
layers.content:
Almost every companion has a conversion scene. Asma does not, and she is the one who tells us why.

Ibn Sa'd carries her sentence through a chain reaching Ibrahim ibn Abd ar-Rahman ibn Abdullah ibn Abi Rabi'a: my father was the first of the Muslims to become Muslim, and by Allah, I only knew my father when he was following the deen. Aishah said nearly the same of both parents, and added that no day at all went by without the Messenger of Allah ﷺ coming to them morning and evening.

So there was no moment of decision to record. She was among the earliest Muslims in Makkah because she grew up inside the room where it began.

The cost arrived from her mother's side of the family. Her grandfather Abu Quhafa was still a mushrik and still in Makkah. Her mother Qutayla was a mushrikah. In that city, being early did not mean joining a movement. For most of those thirteen years it meant being counted, watched and eventually hunted by your own relatives.

Ibn Sa'd also records the shape of the household budget. Abu Bakr had forty thousand dirhams on the day he became Muslim. He spent them freeing and strengthening Muslims until he arrived in Madinah with five thousand. Asma spent her girlhood watching a fortune be taken apart on purpose.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III — narrated from Asma bint Abi Bakr, and the reports on Abu Bakr's wealth

layers.title: With the Prophet ﷺ
layers.subtitle: A cut belt, a food bag, and a broken earring
layers.content:
She was young, newly married, and pregnant during the three days that decided everything.

Hisham ibn Urwa transmits his father's account of the cave of Thawr. Her brother Abdullah carried the news of Makkah up the mountain at night and was back among the Quraysh by morning as though he had never left. Amir ibn Fuhayra grazed Abu Bakr's sheep past the mouth of the cave and gave the two men milk to drink. And Asma cooked and sent food up with him.

Then comes a detail no one would think to invent. She put the food in one bag and found nothing to tie it with, so she cut her belt in two and tied it with that. Which is why, the report ends, she is called the one with two belts.

Before that, the search had already reached her. Quraysh took Ali to the Ka'bah and beat him for an hour and got nothing. Then they came to her door, and Abu Jahl struck her across the face so hard that her earring broke. She still did not tell him where her father had gone.

Days later, verses composed by Abu Ma'bad about a traveller who had passed through the desert began circulating in Makkah. It was Asma who listened to the poem and worked out from it that the two of them were making for Madinah.
layers.hadith_ref: Reported from Hisham ibn Urwa from his father — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III, the section on the Cave and the Hijra
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III; the slap of Abu Jahl from Ibn Ishaq, via al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar

layers.title: The Trial
layers.subtitle: Over ninety, blind, and asked to give up a son
layers.content:
Sixty years after the cave, the last of that generation was still alive, and the same kind of question came back to her door.

Her son Abdullah ibn az-Zubayr had been given the bay'ah in the Hijaz and was besieged in Makkah by al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf on behalf of the Umayyad state. Asma by then was blind and past ninety. The historians of the fitna — at-Tabari, and after him Ibn Kathir — record that Abdullah came to her when the position was hopeless, and that she did not tell him to save himself.

The transmissions differ in their wording, and it is honest to say so. Their sense is consistent. If you know you are upon the truth, she told him, then go forward, and do not let the boys of Banu Umayyah toy with you. But if you wanted this world, you are a wretched son who has destroyed himself and the men with him. He said he feared they would mutilate his body. She answered that a slaughtered sheep takes no hurt from the skinning.

He went out and was killed, and his body was strung up, and she was brought to look at it.

None of this sits in Ibn Sa'd's Vol. III, which closes with the men of Badr. It belongs to the later historians, and it is reported with the ordinary unevenness of their material.
layers.source: at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir on the siege of Makkah, 73 AH — reports differ in wording; not carried in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III

layers.title: The Legacy
layers.subtitle: The earring broke; she did not
layers.content:
Sahih Muslim preserves what she said to al-Hajjaj when he came to her afterwards. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ told us, she said, that in Thaqif there would be a liar and a destroyer of many. The liar we have already seen. As for the destroyer, I do not think you are anyone but him.

She did not long outlive her son. Reports differ on the interval and on her age, which is usually put at close to a hundred, and she is remembered as among the last of the Muhajirun to die.

Vol. III catches her in a quieter register. When Umar organised the first stipends of the Muslim state, he wrote out allowances for the earliest of the Muhajirun women — Asma bint Umays, Asma bint Abi Bakr, and Umm Abd, the mother of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud — a thousand dirhams each. A treasury was now paying a pension to the girl who had once torn her belt in half to tie up a food bag.

What the ummah kept from her, may Allah be pleased with her, is not an office or a book. It is a temperament. Twice a man with the power to hurt her put a question to her: where is your father, and will you tell your son to surrender. Both answers cost her something. Both times she gave the same kind of answer.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih Muslim, Book of the Virtues of the Companions — narrated by Asma bint Abi Bakr: the Prophet ﷺ said that in Thaqif there would be a liar and a great destroyer
layers.source: Sahih Muslim (not carried in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III); Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III for Umar's register of stipends

quiz.prompt: Why is Asma bint Abi Bakr called Dhat an-Nitaqayn, she of the two belts?

options.text: She wore two belts as a sign of her clan
She cut her belt in two to tie the food bag she sent to the cave
She carried two water skins on the Hijrah
Her father gave her two belts on her wedding day

quiz.citation: Reported from Hisham ibn Urwa from his father — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: She had packed food and had nothing to fasten the bag with. The improvisation of one anxious evening became the name she is known by for fourteen centuries.

quiz.prompt: What happened when Quraysh came to her door hunting for her father?

options.text: She sent them towards Yemen with a false trail
Abu Jahl struck her so hard that her earring broke
They took her to the Ka'bah and confined her
Her grandfather Abu Quhafa turned them away

quiz.citation: Ibn Ishaq, via al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the Hijrah
quiz.scholar_reflection: They had already beaten Ali at the Ka'bah without result. She was the second attempt, and she gave them nothing either.

quiz.prompt: How did Asma describe her own beginning in Islam?

options.text: That she believed on the night her father did
That she hesitated until the Hijrah
That she only ever knew her father as a man following the deen
That she accepted Islam at the hands of Khadijah

quiz.citation: Narrated from Asma bint Abi Bakr — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: She had no conversion story to tell, because there was no version of her father she remembered from before. Aishah described their parents in almost identical words.

quiz.prompt: At the end of her life, what did Asma say to her son Abdullah ibn az-Zubayr while he was besieged in Makkah?

options.text: That he should accept terms and preserve the family
That if he knew he was upon the truth he should go forward
That she would go out and negotiate with al-Hajjaj herself
That he should leave for Madinah under cover of night

quiz.citation: at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir on the siege of Makkah, 73 AH — reports differ in wording; not in Ibn Sa'd Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: She attached a condition to it, which is the part usually left out: if you were only after this world, then you are a wretched son. She asked him to be certain before she asked him to be brave.

quiz.prompt: How does Ibn Sa'd's Vol. III record her in the register of Umar's first stipends?

options.text: Among the wives of the Prophet ﷺ at ten thousand dirhams
Among the earliest Muhajirun women at a thousand dirhams
Among the people of Badr at six thousand dirhams
She refused a stipend and was not entered

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III — Umar's allotment of stipends
quiz.scholar_reflection: The entry lists her beside Asma bint Umays and the mother of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud. Three women who had carried the religion when it had no treasury were now line items in one.

quiz.prompt: She was asked where her father was by a man who could hit her, and she did not answer. What actually moves you off the truth when you are under pressure?

options.text: Fear of physical or financial harm
Wanting the confrontation to be over
Fear of being disliked more than fear of being hurt
Very little, and I have been tested enough to know

quiz.citation: Reflection on Ibn Ishaq's account of Abu Jahl at her door, via al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: Silence was an option that would have satisfied nobody and cost her a blow. She chose it in the seconds she had, which suggests she had decided in advance.

quiz.prompt: She never had a conversion story — she only ever knew her father as a believer. Did your faith come to you as a choice, or as an inheritance?

options.text: Inherited, and I have never really examined it
Inherited, then chosen again later on my own terms
Chosen against what I was raised with
I am still in the middle of working that out

quiz.citation: Narrated from Asma bint Abi Bakr — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Being raised inside something is not the same as having nothing at stake. She grew up watching what it cost her father, in money and in safety, year after year.

quiz.prompt: Her contribution to the Hijrah was cooking, packing and keeping quiet. Which kind of usefulness comes more naturally to you?

options.text: The work nobody sees, and I prefer it that way
Visible work — I want my effort attached to my name
Whatever is needed, though I notice when it goes unremarked
I am better at logistics than at anything public

quiz.citation: Reflection on Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III — the section on the Cave and the Hijra
quiz.scholar_reflection: The two most consequential nights in the history of the religion were provisioned by a young woman with a bag and a torn belt. The bag is what made the belt famous.

quiz.prompt: At over ninety she told her son to go out to a death rather than a surrender. Where is the edge of what you would ask of someone you love?
quiz.slider_label: What you would ask of your own

options.text: I would always choose their safety first
I would ask it, but only if they were already certain
I could not say the words, whatever I believed
I do not know, and I hope never to find out

quiz.citation: Reflection on the accounts of the siege of Makkah, 73 AH, in at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir
quiz.scholar_reflection: Note that she did not tell him he was right. She told him to establish whether he was, and then to act accordingly. That is a harder thing to say than encouragement.

quiz.prompt: Her life stretched from the cave outside Makkah to a siege of the same city sixty years later. What do you expect to still be carrying decades from now?

options.text: My faith, and probably very little else
The people — everything else seems to move
I rarely think past the next year or two
Habits, which will have quietly decided the rest

quiz.citation: Reflection on the life of Asma bint Abi Bakr, in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III and the later historians
quiz.scholar_reflection: She outlived her father, her husband, her sister, and her son. What survived in her across all of it was not a position but a way of answering questions.
